reels.title: Counting what never stops

beats.say: How do you count something that never stops happening?

A batch job is like counting cars in a car park after it closes. The lot is full, nothing moves, you finish and go home. A stream is a motorway at rush hour. There is no closing time. So you count in slices, say one minute at a time, and you must decide when a slice is done.

chip.text: No end, so count in slices

beats.say: Then there is the postcard problem. A postcard has the day it was written and the day it arrived. A rider in a tunnel writes now, but the card lands ten minutes later. Which day should count?
Last, the counter works for months. If the guard changes shift, the new guard needs the notes, or the count starts again at zero.

show.title: A counter that never retires
items: Keep notes so the count survives

check.q: Why is counting a stream harder than counting a closed car park?
opts: There is no closing time, so you must cut slices and decide when each is done
check.why: A stream has no natural end, so you must choose slice boundaries and when a slice is finished. That is the root of every other streaming problem.

work: Pick one metric at work and say what slice size it would need if it were live.
Ask which of your numbers are counted by arrival time rather than by when things happened.

reels.title: Windows, two clocks and watermarks

beats.say: Surge pricing needs rider counts per zone, right now. Why can't last hour's batch job do it?
Because a batch job reads a fixed file and stops. A stream never ends, so we cut it into windows, for example one minute each, and count requests per zone per window.

Each event carries two times. Event time is when the rider tapped the phone. Processing time is when our job saw it. A phone in a tunnel can be five minutes late. Count by processing time, and the nine o'clock window holds whatever happened to arrive.
So we use event time, plus a watermark. That is a marker saying nothing older than, say, two minutes is still coming. When it passes the window's end, we emit the count.

check.q: A rider taps at 9:00 but the event reaches the job at 9:05. Which window should count it for surge pricing?
check.why: Event time reflects what really happened. Processing time would shift the count into the wrong window whenever the network is slow.

work: For each streaming job you own, write down which clock its windows use.
Find the field that holds event time and check it is set on the device, not the server.

reels.title: Crashes, late data and growing state

beats.say: Your job crashed at three in the morning with forty thousand half-finished counts in memory. What happens now?

Without protection, those counts vanish and the job restarts from the wrong place. So the engine takes a checkpoint every thirty seconds. It saves the state and the input position, such as the Kafka offset, together. On restart it reloads both and carries on.

Now the watermark trap. Set it two minutes behind and every answer waits two minutes. Set it tight and tunnel events arrive after their window closed. Those are late events. You must choose: drop them, update the result, or send them to a side output.
Last gotcha: state grows. A window kept open for a day across a million riders can exhaust memory, so always set an expiry on state.

show.title: State needs a time to live

check.q: Why does a checkpoint save the input offset together with the counts?
opts: So a restart does not double count or skip events
check.why: If counts and position were saved at different moments, a restart would replay events already counted or skip events never counted.

work: Check how often your job checkpoints and how long recovery takes in a test.
Decide and document what happens to events later than the watermark.
Set a time to live on every keyed state store.

reels.title: When streaming is worth the bill

beats.say: Do you really need streaming, or does it just feel modern?

show.text: Need it, or just like it?

beats.say: Streaming costs more. You run servers around the clock, hold state, and keep people on call for restarts and lag. A batch job runs for ten minutes and then costs nothing.

So start from the latency the business needs. Surge pricing needs seconds, so stream. A daily finance report needs hours, so batch. If five minutes is fine, a micro-batch job every five minutes is far simpler.

When you do stream, set the watermark by the cost of being wrong. A slightly wrong surge price for a minute is cheap, so use a short watermark. Billing is not cheap, so stream for speed, then reconcile with a batch job overnight.

show.title: Match accuracy to risk
items: Stream for speed, batch for truth

check.q: A dashboard only needs to be fresh within ten minutes. What is the best choice?
opts: A micro-batch job every few minutes
check.why: Micro-batch meets a ten minute need with far less state, on-call load and cost than an always-on stream.

work: List your pipelines with the freshness the business really needs, not what was asked for.
Move any stream whose users accept minutes of delay to micro-batch.
Add a nightly batch reconciliation for money-related streams.

reels.title: A table that keeps growing

beats.say: What if a never-ending stream of data could be treated like a spreadsheet that just keeps getting new rows?

show.text: A stream is a table that keeps growing
show.sub: new rows arrive all the time

beats.say: That is Structured Streaming. Picture a clerk with a growing ledger. Every ten seconds, the clerk reads only the new lines added since last time, and updates the totals.
The clerk keeps a bookmark showing where they stopped. If they go home sick, the next clerk reads the bookmark and carries on. Nothing is lost, and nothing is counted twice.
You write the same code you would for a fixed table. The engine does the repeating for you.

show.title: Why it feels easy
items: Engine repeats it for new rows

check.q: In the analogy, what does the bookmark protect against?
opts: Losing or double counting rows after a crash
check.why: The bookmark is the checkpoint: it records where processing stopped so a restart continues from there without gaps or repeats.

work: Explain to a colleague why a stream can be seen as an unbounded table.
Find one batch job of yours that could be rewritten as a streaming query with almost no code change.

reels.title: Micro-batches and the checkpoint

beats.say: How does a streaming job read Kafka without ever losing its place?

show.text: Where does Spark remember its place?

beats.say: Every ten seconds, Spark starts a small batch. It reads the new Kafka records, up to fifty thousand, because max offsets per trigger sets that cap.
Spark also writes to the checkpoint, a folder in durable storage like S3. It stores which offsets the batch covered, plus the running state.

On restart, Spark reads the checkpoint and continues from there. It ignores Kafka consumer group commits. After a long outage, the cap makes it chew the backlog in steady fifty thousand record pieces, instead of choking on millions at once.

check.q: Where does Structured Streaming track which Kafka offsets it has processed?
check.why: Spark stores offsets and state in its own checkpoint. Kafka consumer group commits are not used for its progress.

work: Put every query's checkpoint on durable storage with a unique path per query.
Set max offsets per trigger so a restart after an outage does not overload the cluster.

reels.title: Windows and the watermark

beats.say: How can a job count requests per minute forever without running out of memory?

show.text: Counting forever needs a way to forget

beats.say: It keeps a running count for each open one minute window. A tumbling window is fixed, like each minute. A sliding one overlaps. A session window closes after a gap in activity.

show.title: Window types
items: Session: closes after a quiet gap

beats.say: The watermark limits the memory. Spark tracks the latest event time seen, and subtracts two minutes. Say the latest is twelve ten. The watermark is twelve oh eight.
Any window ending before twelve oh eight is final, and Spark frees its memory. An event arriving later than that is dropped. A longer watermark accepts more late data, but holds more state.

check.q: The latest event time seen is 12:10 and the watermark delay is 2 minutes. What happens to a window ending at 12:07?
opts: It stays open for more events
It is final and its state is freed
check.why: The watermark is 12:08. Windows ending before it are final, so Spark frees their state and drops later events for them.

work: Ask the business how late data can be before choosing a watermark.
Monitor state size per query so a long watermark does not surprise you.

reels.title: Output modes and freshness

beats.say: Your dashboard needs data within thirty seconds, but your append query shows each minute about three minutes late. Why?
Append mode writes only final windows. A one minute window with a two minute watermark becomes final about three minutes in. After that, the row never changes.
Update mode writes every window whose count changed, so it is fresh within one batch. The catch is that rows get revised when late events arrive.
Complete mode rewrites the whole result table every batch, so keep it for tiny results. Surge pricing wants update. Finance wants append. The same stream can feed both.

show.title: Pick by need
items: Append: final, late by about 3 minutes

check.q: Surge pricing needs numbers within 30 seconds and can tolerate revisions. Which mode fits?
check.why: Update emits changed windows every batch, so it is fresh. Append waits for finality and complete rewrites everything.

work: For each consumer of a stream, write down whether it wants fresh or final numbers.
Check whether any dashboard silently relies on append and is therefore minutes behind.

reels.title: At-least-once and idempotent merges

beats.say: Your job crashes after writing to the table but before saving its checkpoint. Do you get duplicates?
Iceberg sinks accept append and complete only. For update behavior, use foreachBatch, which hands you each micro batch as an ordinary DataFrame.

show.title: foreachBatch
show.note: each micro-batch is a normal DataFrame

beats.say: But foreachBatch is at least once. Spark never recorded the batch as done, so on restart it runs the same batch again.

The fix is a merge keyed on window start and zone id. Rerun the batch and the same rows are overwritten with the same counts. Harmless. Never delete the checkpoint, though. That makes the query forget everything.

show.title: Make replays safe
items: MERGE on window start and zone id

check.q: Why is a MERGE on (window_start, zone_id) safe inside foreachBatch?
opts: Replaying a batch rewrites the same rows with the same values
It removes the need for a checkpoint
check.why: foreachBatch is at-least-once, so replays happen. An idempotent keyed merge makes a replay produce the same final table.

work: Make every foreachBatch write idempotent, using a merge or a delete-then-insert on a key.
Test a replay by killing the job mid-batch and confirming counts are unchanged.

reels.title: When to choose Structured Streaming

beats.say: When is Structured Streaming the wrong tool?

show.text: When is it the wrong tool?

beats.say: The watermark is a business decision. Two minutes means later data is silently lost. Ten minutes accepts more, but holds about five times more window state in memory.
Micro-batches add latency of at least a batch interval, ten seconds here. If you need sub-second response, consider an event at a time engine such as Flink.
If a nightly report is enough, a plain batch job is cheaper than a cluster running all day. Otherwise, serve fresh update rows to pricing and final append rows to finance, from one stream.

show.title: Decide
items: Sub-second: event at a time engine
One stream can feed fresh and final outputs

check.q: A fraud team needs decisions in under 100 milliseconds per event. What is the best fit?
opts: Structured Streaming with a 10 second trigger
An event at a time engine
check.why: Micro-batches have a latency floor of the trigger interval. Sub-second needs a per-event engine.

work: Write down the latency target and lateness tolerance before picking an engine.
Price a always-on streaming cluster against a scheduled batch job for the same output.

reels.title: The order slip nobody told the kitchen about

beats.say: What happens when one person changes the order form and nobody tells the kitchen?

Picture a restaurant. Waiters write orders on slips. The kitchen reads them. Both agree on the layout: table, dish, notes. Then a waiter adds a new box for allergies. The cook has never seen it, and orders get misread.

So the restaurant keeps a binder at the front desk, with every version of the slip. Each slip carries only a page number. The cook looks up that page and reads correctly. The binder refuses any new layout that would confuse the kitchen.
That binder is a schema registry. A schema is just the agreed shape of a message. The safe habit: every new box gets a default answer, like none.

show.title: Remember
items: Schema = agreed shape of a message
New box = always give a default

check.q: In the restaurant picture, what does the binder at the front desk stand for?
opts: A schema registry that stores every version of the shape
check.why: The binder holds every version of the slip layout, and slips only carry a page number. That is the registry and the schema id.

work: Find one stream at work and ask who agreed on its message shape.
Ask your team whether new fields always get a default value.

reels.title: How a schema id replaces a schema

beats.say: How can a million messages a second all describe their own shape without drowning in overhead?
They don't carry the schema. The producer registers its schema once and gets back a small id, say forty-two. Each message holds only that id, about five bytes, plus the data.
The consumer sees id forty-two, fetches that schema from the registry once, and caches it. After that, no more lookups.

When a producer registers a changed schema, the registry checks it against the topic's compatibility rule. If it breaks the rule, registration is rejected, so the bad version never reaches the stream.

check.q: What does each message on the topic carry to describe its shape?
check.why: Only a small id travels with the data. Consumers fetch the schema from the registry once and cache it.

work: Check how large your schema id header is compared with the payload.
Confirm consumers cache schemas instead of calling the registry per message.

reels.title: Backward, forward, full

beats.say: Backward, forward, full: which one actually protects you, and who must upgrade first?
Backward means the new schema can read old data. You may delete fields, or add fields with defaults. Upgrade consumers first, so they can read both old and new messages.

show.title: Backward
items: Delete fields, or add with defaults

beats.say: Forward means the old schema can read new data. You may add fields, or delete ones that had defaults. Upgrade producers first, since old consumers keep working.

show.title: Forward
items: Add fields, or delete with defaults

beats.say: Full means both. You may only add or delete fields that have defaults. Then you can upgrade in any order.

show.title: Full
items: Only add or delete fields with defaults

beats.say: Backward is the usual default because a consumer can replay old messages from last month using the newest schema.

show.text: Replay old data with the newest schema

check.q: You choose backward compatibility. Which side do you upgrade first?
check.why: Backward means the new schema can read old data. Upgraded consumers handle both old and new messages, so they go first.

work: Look up the compatibility mode on your busiest topic.
Write down who must upgrade first for that mode.

reels.title: When the registry says yes and it still breaks

beats.say: You added a field, the registry said yes, and the numbers are still wrong. How?
The registry checks shape, not meaning. If price changes from dollars to cents, the type is still a number, so the registry approves it. Every total is silently wrong by a hundred times.
Changing a field's type is the other trap. A number turned into text cannot be read by the old schema, or replayed from old data.

show.title: Type changes
items: Number to text breaks old readers
Replay of old data breaks too

beats.say: A rename looks harmless, but it is really a delete plus an add. Without a default on the new name, old data cannot be read.

show.title: Renames
items: Old data has no value for it

beats.say: The fix: give every new field a default, and never change a type or meaning. Make a new field instead.

show.text: Default always. Never change type or meaning.

check.q: A field called price changes from dollars to cents, still an integer. What happens?
opts: The registry rejects it as a type change
The registry accepts it and totals silently go wrong
Consumers crash with a schema error
check.why: Compatibility rules check structure, not meaning. The shape is unchanged, so it passes while the data is wrong.

work: Add a review step for meaning changes, not just shape changes.
Ship changed meaning as a new field name with a default.

reels.title: Choosing a mode and handling breaking change

beats.say: When is a schema registry more trouble than it is worth, and what do you do when you must truly break the schema?
Pick the mode by who you control. If you own the consumers and want replay, use backward. If many teams read your topic and cannot upgrade quickly, use full, so any order works.
The cost is another service. Cache schemas in clients so an outage only hurts new schemas, and run it highly available. For one team and one small topic, a registry may be overkill.

show.title: Cost and limits
items: Clients cache, so outage hurts only new schemas

beats.say: For a truly breaking change, don't force it. Create a new topic with the new schema, write to both for a while, move consumers across, then retire the old one.

check.q: Many independent teams consume your topic and upgrade on their own schedules. Which mode fits best?
check.why: Full works in both directions, so producers and consumers can upgrade in any order without coordination.

work: Map each shared topic to its consumers and pick the mode by who can upgrade.
Write a runbook for breaking changes using a new topic and dual writes.

reels.title: Three ways to sort a never-ending stream

beats.say: How do you sort a never-ending stream of parcels? There are three common ways, and each streaming tool picks one.
Spark Structured Streaming is a shuttle bus. It waits a few seconds, gathers everyone at the stop, then drives off with the whole group. Simple and efficient, but you wait for the bus.

chip.text: Wait a few seconds, then go

beats.say: Flink is a conveyor belt. Each parcel is handled the moment it arrives, so the delay is milliseconds. But it needs its own factory to run in, called a cluster.
Kafka Streams is a helper who sits inside your own shop. No separate factory. It reads parcels from the Kafka mailroom and hands the results straight back.

show.title: Kafka Streams is a *helper in your shop*

check.q: Which tool is like a library that lives inside your own service, with no separate cluster?
check.why: Kafka Streams is a library you embed in your application. Spark runs as a Spark application and Flink runs as its own cluster.

work: Write one sentence on how you would explain bus versus conveyor belt to a non-technical colleague.
List which of your current pipelines wait for a batch and which react to each event.

reels.title: Why seconds versus milliseconds

beats.say: Why does one streaming tool answer in seconds while another answers in milliseconds?

show.sub: Where does the wait come from?

beats.say: By default Spark cuts the stream into micro-batches. Every two seconds, say, it reads the new rows, runs the job, and writes a checkpoint. A checkpoint is a saved record of progress so the job can restart. Latency is the interval plus processing time, so seconds.
Flink and Kafka Streams handle one event at a time. An event arrives, updates its running count, and moves on right away. That is why you see milliseconds.

That running count is state, the memory of the job. Flink manages very large state and takes savepoints, which are deliberate snapshots. Kafka Streams keeps state in local stores, backed up to Kafka topics.

check.q: Why does default Spark Structured Streaming show latency in seconds?
opts: It processes rows in micro-batches, so rows wait for the interval and the job
check.why: Rows wait for the batch window to close and then for the job to run, so latency is roughly interval plus processing time.

work: Check the trigger interval on one of your Spark streaming jobs and compare it to your latency goal.
Name the biggest piece of state in a streaming job you own and where it is stored.

reels.title: Real-Time Mode and state recovery

beats.say: If Spark batches rows, how can it ever answer in milliseconds?

Databricks Real-Time Mode changes execution. It became generally available for Structured Streaming in early 2026, and for Declarative Pipelines in October. All stages run at once, and each row is passed on as soon as it is produced.

Before, every row waited for the whole batch to finish. That wait made the seconds. Removing it gives milliseconds, but processors stay busy all the time, and Photon is not supported, so it costs more.

show.title: The trade
items: Old: rows wait for the whole batch

beats.say: A gotcha with Kafka Streams. Its state is a local store. If the instance dies, a new one rebuilds it by replaying the backing topic, so recovery is slow when state is large.

check.q: A Kafka Streams instance dies and a new one starts. How does it get its state back?
opts: It replays the backing topic into a new store
It loads the latest Flink savepoint from S3 storage
It starts empty and ignores every past event
check.why: Local stores are backed by Kafka topics, so a replacement replays that topic, which takes longer with large state.

work: Estimate recovery time for your largest stateful job after a crash.
Ask what extra compute an always-on low latency mode would add to your bill.

reels.title: Choosing the engine and the architecture

beats.say: When is a faster engine worth paying for, and when is it waste?

show.text: Pay for speed only when it pays back

beats.say: Ask one question: does a sub-second number change a decision? Blocking a fraudulent payment, yes. A demand count refreshed every few seconds, no. Then micro-batches are cheaper and simpler, especially if your team already runs Spark.

Match the tool to its home. Flink suits low latency, tricky event-time logic and very large state, such as change data capture. Kafka Streams suits Kafka-to-Kafka work inside a microservice. Spark suits shared batch and stream code and lakehouse sinks.

show.title: Best fit
items: Flink: low latency, event time, huge state
Kafka Streams: Kafka to Kafka in a service

beats.say: Lambda runs batch and streaming side by side, so you write the logic twice and the two drift apart. Kappa uses one streaming pipeline and replays the log when logic changes. A lakehouse with streaming writes is close to kappa.

chip.text: One codebase is easier to keep correct

check.q: A team already runs Spark and needs demand counts refreshed every few seconds. What is the best default?
check.why: Seconds of latency is enough, so cheaper and simpler micro-batches on the existing platform win. Lambda would mean writing logic twice.

work: For each streaming use case, write the decision that a faster answer would change.
Find any pipeline where logic is duplicated across batch and streaming and plan to merge it.

reels.title: The librarian who fetches pages

beats.say: How can an assistant answer questions about documents it has never read? It does not read the whole library. It fetches the right page first.
Picture a new engineer on call. Nobody hands them every document in the company. They ask a librarian, who comes back with the three pages that match the question.
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, works the same way. The system finds the few relevant passages, then hands them to the AI model along with your question.

chip.text: Question plus passages go in together

beats.say: So the answer is grounded in your own runbooks, and it can name which page it used. Without that, the model only guesses from general knowledge.

show.title: Why it matters
items: Answers come from your own documents
It can name the source page

check.q: Why does RAG fetch only a few passages instead of giving the model every document?
opts: Sending everything is wasteful and soon impossible, so only relevant passages are fetched
Passages are always more accurate than full documents
check.why: Putting every document in every prompt wastes effort and quickly stops fitting. Fetching just the relevant passages at question time solves both.

work: List the documents your on-call engineers actually ask about: runbooks, schema notes, incident write-ups.
Pick one recent question a teammate asked and note which page answered it.

reels.title: From question to cited answer

beats.say: A runbook set has hundreds of pages. How does a question about lag find the one right paragraph in a fraction of a second?

First, chunk: split at headings, so each chunk is one complete procedure with its title. Then an embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, a list of numbers, where similar meaning gives nearby numbers.

Store each vector with its text and source. At question time, embed the question the same way and take the four nearest chunks. Nearness is cosine similarity, a score for how closely two vectors point the same way.
Finally, the model gets the question plus those four chunks. Require it to cite the source of every claim, and to say so when the chunks do not contain the answer.

steps.label: Say when the answer is missing

check.q: At question time, what is done with the question before finding chunks?
opts: It is embedded with the same model and compared to the stored vectors
It is deleted after the model reads it
check.why: The question must live in the same vector space as the chunks, so the same embedding model turns it into a vector, and the nearest stored vectors win.

work: Split one runbook at its headings and check each chunk stands alone with its title.
Prompt the model to cite a source per claim and to say when the chunks lack the answer.

reels.title: Why retrieval quietly fails

beats.say: Your agent answers with confidence, and the answer is wrong. Is the model to blame? Often the right chunk never reached it.

show.text: Wrong chunk in, wrong answer out

beats.say: Retrieval is search, so test it as search. Write ten questions and note which chunk should answer each. Count how often that chunk lands in the top four. If it misses, no prompt can rescue the answer.

show.title: Hit rate in the top four

beats.say: Embeddings also blur exact terms. An identifier like max dot poll dot interval dot ms, or an error code, carries little meaning to capture, so a vaguely related chunk can outrank the real one.
Hybrid search runs keyword search alongside vector search and merges the results. Keywords catch exact identifiers. Vectors catch paraphrases. Together they fix much of the problem.

check.q: Your agent keeps giving wrong answers about a specific error code. What should you check first?
opts: Whether the correct chunk appears in the top four retrieved results
check.why: If retrieval misses the right chunk, no prompt or model change can fix it. Measure the hit rate, and consider hybrid search for exact identifiers.

work: Write ten real questions with the chunk that should answer each, and track the top-four hit rate.
Add keyword search for identifiers and error codes, then rerun the same ten questions.

reels.title: Retrieval or a tool?

beats.say: Your agent is asked for the current consumer lag. Should it search the runbooks?

show.sub: search a document, or ask the system?

beats.say: No. Retrieval returns prose written earlier, so it hands back yesterday's document. Live facts, like current lag or today's row count, belong to a tool that queries the system right now.

chip.text: Live number means call a tool

beats.say: Scale shapes the build. For a few hundred chunks, an array in memory is plenty. A vector database earns its cost at millions of chunks, or when you need filtering and frequent updates.
So choose by kind of knowledge and by size. Prose goes to retrieval, live numbers go to tools, and start with the simplest store that works.

check.q: A user asks the agent for today's row count in a table. What is the best design?
opts: Call a tool that queries the table now
Add the table's history to every prompt
check.why: Retrieval returns written documents, which are stale for live values. A tool reads the current state directly.

work: Sort your agent's questions into prose knowledge versus live facts, and route each to retrieval or a tool.
Start with an in-memory array and move to a vector database only when size, filtering or updates demand it.

reels.title: The letter nobody can read

beats.say: What happens when one letter in a huge pile of mail is impossible to read?

show.sub: What happens to everything behind it?

beats.say: Picture a mail sorter at a post office. Letters ride a belt to him. One is smudged, so he cannot read the address. He keeps trying again and again. Meanwhile, the belt behind him piles up with letters.
A smart sorter drops that letter into a special tray, writes a note saying what went wrong, and keeps going. A manager is told about the tray.
Later, someone fixes the cause and puts those letters back on the belt. In data work, that tray is called a dead-letter topic. The pile behind is called lag.

show.title: Words to remember
items: Dead-letter topic: the tray for records that fail
Lag: how far behind the reader is
Replay: put fixed items back on the belt

check.q: A record can never be parsed. What is the best way to treat it?
opts: Retry it forever until it works
Set it aside with the error, keep going, and alert
check.why: Retrying forever stalls everything behind it. Silent deletion loses data. A side tray with the error keeps the flow moving and lets you fix and replay later.

work: Find out what your streaming jobs do today when one record fails to parse.
Ask who gets alerted if a record is set aside.

reels.title: Dead-letter topic in action

beats.say: One broken record. A job that retries it forever. What does that cost you?

Say a partition gets one thousand records a second. Record number forty two thousand cannot be parsed. The consumer fails, retries, fails again. It cannot move past that offset, so after one minute, lag is sixty thousand records.
The fix: catch the parse error, write the original bytes and the error message to a dead-letter topic, commit the offset, and move on. Then alert when that topic receives records.
Once engineers fix the cause, they replay the dead-letter topic back through the job.

check.q: Why does one unparseable record make lag grow on its partition?
opts: The consumer cannot move past its offset while it keeps retrying
Kafka deletes the records behind it
check.why: Offsets are processed in order. If the consumer is stuck retrying one offset, nothing after it is read, so lag grows.

work: Add a catch block that writes original bytes and the error to a dead-letter topic.
Create an alert on dead-letter topic message count.

reels.title: Lag is rising: what first?

beats.say: Lag grows steadily every minute. Where do you look first?

show.sub: The consumer is slower than the producer

beats.say: Start with the cheapest check: a rebalance loop. That is when consumers keep leaving and rejoining the group, so nobody does real work. Fix timeouts and crashes first.

Second, make each record cheaper. For example, batch database writes instead of one call per record. Third, add consumers, but only up to the partition count. Each partition feeds one consumer in a group, so extras sit idle.
Only last, add partitions. That raises the ceiling, but it changes which partition a key lands on.

check.q: A topic has 8 partitions and 8 busy consumers. Lag still rises. What does adding a 9th consumer do?
opts: Speeds things up by one ninth
check.why: A partition is read by one consumer in a group, so the ninth has nothing to read. Speed up processing or add partitions.

work: Check rebalance counts before you scale anything.
Write down your partition count next to each consumer group.

reels.title: Replay without double counting

beats.say: You fixed a bug. Can you just rerun last week's data?

show.sub: Replaying safely is the hard part

beats.say: Replay means restarting from an older offset with a new checkpoint, so the job forgets where it was. Every old message flows through again.
The danger is duplicates. If the sink appends rows or sends emails, you do it twice. An idempotent sink, like an upsert by key, gives the same result however many times it runs.

show.title: Idempotent sink
items: Upsert by key equals same result
Emails and payments need dedupe keys

beats.say: Write the steps in a runbook before you need them. Stop the job, pick the offset, set a new checkpoint, restart, then verify counts.

check.q: Why must the sink be idempotent before you replay?
opts: Replayed messages are processed again and could be written twice
check.why: Replay re-sends messages already handled. Without idempotent writes, such as upserts by key, results are duplicated.

work: Check whether each sink uses upsert or append.
Write and rehearse a replay runbook in a test environment.

reels.title: Not every failure is poison

beats.say: Is every failed record a poison message?

show.sub: Retrying the wrong failure is costly

beats.say: A database timeout is temporary, so a few retries with a pause will work. A bad format is permanent and fails every time. Retrying that only stalls the partition.
So classify errors. Retry temporary ones a limited number of times, then dead-letter. Keep the original bytes, not just the parsed result, or you cannot replay after fixing the parser.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Store original bytes plus the error

beats.say: Also alert on the rate. A sudden flood in the dead-letter topic usually means an upstream schema change, not bad luck.

check.q: Why store the original bytes in the dead-letter record?
opts: You can replay after fixing the parser
It speeds up the main job
check.why: If only a partly parsed form is saved, you cannot reprocess it once the parser is fixed. The raw bytes keep every option open.

work: Separate retryable errors from permanent ones in your error handler.
Set dead-letter topic retention longer than your fix time.

reels.title: Skip, halt, or scale: the trade-offs

beats.say: Dead-letter everything and sleep well? Not quite.
Skipping a record means that data is missing downstream until replayed. Where completeness or order matters, such as account balances, you may prefer to halt and page someone.

show.title: Choose by cost of a gap

beats.say: Adding consumers costs money and stops helping at the partition count. Adding partitions is hard to undo and changes where existing keys land, which can break per-key order. Size partitions with headroom early.

show.title: Scaling limits
items: More partitions cannot be removed later

beats.say: Set a threshold too. If more than about one percent of records fail, stop the job, because that signals a systemic fault, not a few bad records.

check.q: Which pipeline most justifies halting on a bad record instead of dead-lettering it?
opts: Page view counts for a dashboard
check.why: A skipped ledger entry makes balances wrong, so correctness outweighs availability. Analytics can tolerate a temporary gap.

work: Classify each pipeline as skip-and-alert or halt, and record why.
Add a failure-rate threshold that stops the job automatically.

reels.title: Kafka as a shared notebook

beats.say: What if every message you sent was kept, and anyone could read it later, at their own speed?
Picture a big notebook at a bakery. Each baker writes what they baked on a new line at the bottom. Nothing is ever erased.
Staff each keep a bookmark. The driver reads fast. The accountant reads once a day. Each bookmark moves on its own, and the bakers never need to know who is reading.
A new hire can start from page one and catch up. That notebook is Kafka: a shared, durable log that separates the writers from the readers.

check.q: Why can a brand new team read last week's events from Kafka?
opts: Messages are kept after being read
Consumers store a copy of everything
check.why: Kafka is a log: reading does not delete, so a new consumer can start from an earlier position.

work: List the teams that would want to read the same stream of events.
Ask which of your queues delete messages that a new team might later need.

reels.title: Why Kafka is fast on disk

beats.say: Kafka writes every message to disk, so why is it fast?
A disk is slow when its head jumps around, which is called seeking. Kafka only adds to the end of a file, so the disk writes in one straight line.

Reads mostly come from memory. The operating system keeps recent data in its page cache, and zero copy sends it from there straight to the network, skipping the application. One catch: with TLS the broker must encrypt each byte itself, so that shortcut is lost.

chip.text: Zero copy, no app in between

beats.say: Producers also batch and compress. One thousand small messages become one write and one network call. Most reads never touch the disk at all.

check.q: Which choice best explains why Kafka's disk writes are fast?
opts: It keeps every message only in the JVM heap
It appends sequentially and avoids seeking
It spreads each message over a different disk
check.why: Appending to the end of a log gives sequential writes, which disks handle far faster than random ones.

work: Raise batch size and linger on a producer and compare throughput.
Leave spare RAM on brokers for the page cache rather than a huge heap.

reels.title: Partitions cap parallelism

beats.say: Why can adding consumers fail to make Kafka faster?
A topic is split into partitions. Say it has six. In a classic consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer.

chip.text: Each partition has one reader per group

beats.say: So six consumers is the ceiling, and a seventh sits idle. Kafka 4.2 made share groups generally available: many consumers take records from one partition, like a queue, acknowledging each one. The catch is that order within a key is lost.
Keys keep order because the same key lands on one partition. But if one customer sends half the traffic, that partition is hot, and its consumer falls behind.

check.q: A topic has 4 partitions and one classic consumer group has 8 consumers. What happens?
check.why: In a classic group each partition goes to one consumer, so at most 4 are active. A share group could use all 8, giving up per-key order.

work: Check the largest key's share of traffic on your busiest topic.
Pick partition counts for the load you expect in a year, not today.
Use a share group only for work where order does not matter.

reels.title: What acks=all really promises

beats.say: With three copies of your data, what does an acknowledged write really promise?
Set acks to all, replication factor three, and min in sync replicas two. The leader answers only after every in-sync replica has the record. It refuses writes if fewer than two are in sync.
So an acknowledged write lives on at least two brokers and survives losing one.

show.title: Guarantee
items: Ack means two or more copies

beats.say: Lose two brokers and producers get a not enough replicas error. Kafka stops accepting writes rather than take data it could lose. Committed data stays readable. Keep unclean leader election off, so a stale replica never becomes leader.

check.q: With RF 3 and min ISR 2, two brokers die. What happens to producers using acks=all?
opts: Writes continue on the last broker
Writes are silently buffered on the leader
check.why: The ISR drops to one, below the minimum of two, so Kafka rejects writes instead of risking data loss.

work: Check that critical topics set min.insync.replicas to 2 with RF 3.
Confirm unclean leader election is off.
Alert on under-replicated partitions.

reels.title: Rebalances and how to calm them

beats.say: Why can one pod restart freeze a whole consumer group?
When a consumer joins, leaves, or misses its heartbeat, the coordinator reassigns partitions. In the old eager protocol, everyone drops everything and waits. The whole group pauses.

Fixes: cooperative sticky assignment, so only the moving partitions pause. Static membership with a group instance id, so a restarting pod gets its partitions back. And in Kafka 4, the new consumer protocol lets the broker plan assignments, but clients must opt in with group protocol set to consumer.
Also keep work per poll under the max poll interval, or Kafka thinks you died. And commit offsets before partitions are revoked, so the next owner does not redo work.

check.q: A pod restarts often during deploys and triggers rebalances. Which helps most?
opts: Static membership with a group instance id
Adding many more partitions to the topic
A much lower consumer heartbeat interval
check.why: Static membership lets the restarted pod reclaim its partitions without a rebalance.

work: Turn on cooperative sticky assignment for consumers.
Set group.instance.id for stateful pods.
Alert on rebalance frequency and poll time.

reels.title: Exactly once and where it stops

beats.say: Kafka says exactly once. So why do duplicates still reach your database?
The idempotent producer numbers each batch per partition, so the broker drops a retried duplicate. Transactions add atomic writes across partitions, plus offset commits.
Consumers set to read committed skip aborted records. Inside Kafka, read, process, write is exactly once.
But the guarantee stops at Kafka's edge. A database or lake sink must be idempotent, such as an upsert by key, or join the same commit, as Flink's two phase sinks do.

check.q: Your consumer writes Kafka events to Postgres and may retry. What makes it safe?
opts: An upsert keyed by event id
check.why: Kafka's guarantee ends at its edge. An idempotent sink write makes retries harmless.

work: Give every event a stable id and use MERGE or upsert in sinks.
Use read_committed where transactions are in play.

reels.title: Should we use Kafka at all?

beats.say: A team proposes Kafka for two hundred events a day. What do you say?

Kafka earns its place when many producers write once and many consumers replay at their own pace. Unlike SQS or RabbitMQ, reading does not delete, so new teams can replay history. Since Kafka 4.2, share groups also give queue-style work sharing on the same log.
Against Kinesis or Pub/Sub you gain Connect, Debezium, Flink and Schema Registry. The price is running it, or paying Confluent or MSK.
Skip it for tiny volumes, request and reply calls, and large files, where you send a pointer to object storage. And skip it if nobody will own the on-call.

show.title: Do not use for
items: Tiny volumes: use a queue or batch
Request and reply: use an API

check.q: Which need is the strongest reason to pick Kafka over SQS?
opts: One worker handling each task once
A quick synchronous request and reply
check.why: Kafka keeps messages after reads, so many consumers can read and replay the same stream independently.

work: Write a one-page decision note: volume, consumers, replay need, owner.
Price managed Kafka against the on-call hours of self-hosting.

reels.title: Owning, paying and leaving Kafka

beats.say: Who pays when Kafka gets expensive, and when do you leave it?

show.text: Own it. Price it. Know the exit.

beats.say: A platform team owns clusters, quotas, access rules, Schema Registry and topic creation. Producing teams own their schemas. Cost per topic, including cross-zone traffic, is shown back to them.
Tiered storage moves old segments to object storage like S3, so months of retention need no extra broker disks, and brokers recover faster. Old reads get slower.

Kafka is the backbone, not the system of record or an analytics engine. Move off when you need only fan-out, when running it costs more than it gives, or when the data is really a table, like Iceberg with change feeds.

show.title: Move off when
items: Ops cost beats value: go managed
Data is really a table that streams

check.q: Retention must grow to one year without buying more broker disks. What fits?
check.why: Tiered storage offloads old segments to cheap object storage, at the cost of slower reads of old data.

work: Tag topics by team and report storage and traffic cost monthly.
Test read speed of tiered data before relying on it for replays.
Review topics that only fan out and could be a queue.

reels.title: Flink: a counter that never stops

beats.say: What do you use when the answer must change every second?
A stream processor reads events as they arrive, keeps a running memory, called state, and updates results straight away. Flink is the best known one: it handles each event the moment it comes in.
Its cousins: Spark Structured Streaming works in small batches every few seconds, and Kafka Streams is a library inside your own service.

show.title: Three engines
items: Flink: event at a time, big state
Spark: micro-batches, one engine for batch too
Kafka Streams: a library, no cluster

beats.say: And sometimes the right engine is none of them: if minutes are fine, a small batch job every five minutes is cheaper and simpler to fix.

check.q: What makes Flink different from Spark Structured Streaming by default?
opts: It handles each event as it arrives
It only reads files from object storage
It cannot keep any state between events
check.why: Flink processes one event at a time; Spark runs micro-batches every few seconds by default.

work: List your streaming jobs and the freshness each consumer really needs.
Mark which could be a five-minute batch job instead.

reels.title: Checkpoints and barriers

beats.say: If a streaming job crashes, how does it avoid counting things twice?
Every so often the sources slip a marker, a barrier, into the stream. When an operator sees the barrier on all its inputs, it saves its state and passes the barrier on.
The checkpoint stores every operator's state plus the source offsets at that barrier, in durable storage such as S3.
After a crash, Flink restores that state and rewinds the sources to those offsets, so every event changes state exactly once.

check.q: What does a checkpoint save together with operator state?
opts: The source offsets at the barrier
A copy of every output record
The job's source code and settings
check.why: State plus the offsets where the barrier was injected let Flink rewind and replay consistently.

work: Find your job's checkpoint interval and storage location.
Check the last checkpoint duration against the interval.

reels.title: Watermarks and late events

beats.say: When is a one-minute window really finished, if events arrive late?
A watermark says: no events older than this time are still coming. Usually it is the newest event time seen, minus an allowed delay, say thirty seconds.
When the watermark passes a window's end, the window fires and its state is cleared. Events that come after that are late: send them to a side output and count them.

show.title: After the watermark
items: Late events go to a side output
Or fire again with allowed lateness

beats.say: One idle partition holds the watermark back for everyone, so windows stop firing. Configure idleness so silent inputs are ignored.

check.q: Why can one idle Kafka partition stop all windows from firing?
opts: The watermark is the minimum across inputs
Flink pauses whenever a broker is idle
Idle partitions delete the window's state
check.why: The overall watermark follows the slowest input, so an idle one holds it back unless idleness is configured.

work: Count late events per day in a side output.
Set source idleness on topics with quiet partitions.

reels.title: Exactly once into a sink

beats.say: Checkpoints protect state. What protects the output?
A two-phase commit sink writes each checkpoint's output inside a transaction, and commits only when that checkpoint completes. If the job fails first, the transaction is aborted and replayed.
Readers must only see committed data, for example Kafka consumers set to read committed.
The catch: results appear only at checkpoint boundaries, so the interval is your latency. Sinks without transactions need idempotent upserts by key instead.

check.q: With a two-phase commit sink, what sets how soon consumers see results?
check.why: Output commits when a checkpoint completes, so the interval sets end-to-end latency.

work: Check that downstream consumers read committed data.
Make sure the sink transaction timeout exceeds the checkpoint interval.

reels.title: State, RocksDB and Flink 2.0

beats.say: Where does a streaming job keep a hundred gigabytes of state?

The heap backend keeps state as objects in memory: fast, but limited by RAM and garbage collection. RocksDB keeps it on local disk with hot data cached, so state can be far larger, with incremental checkpoints.

Flink 2.0 added disaggregated state, called ForSt: the main copy lives in object storage and local disk is only a cache, so checkpoints and rescaling get faster. It is still marked experimental, and it only works with the new asynchronous state API.
Whatever the backend, give state a time to live. A join or window over endless keys grows until checkpoints time out.

check.q: What does Flink 2.0's disaggregated state change?
opts: State is held only on the job manager
The main copy of state lives in object storage
State is never checkpointed at all anymore
check.why: ForSt keeps state in remote storage with local disk as a cache. It is experimental and needs the asynchronous state API.

work: Chart state size per operator over a week.
Add a TTL to any join or window keyed by user or session.
Keep RocksDB for production until disaggregated state leaves experimental.

reels.title: Backpressure and hot keys

beats.say: Lag is growing. Which part of the job is slow?
Backpressure flows upstream: the slowest operator fills its buffers, so everything before it slows and the source falls behind Kafka.
Common causes: too little parallelism, but never more than the topic's partitions; one hot key pinning one subtask; a slow lookup; state without a time to live.

show.title: Usual causes
items: A hot key on one subtask

beats.say: Try both in the simulator: the partitions challenge and the hot key challenge fail in exactly these ways until you fix them.

check.q: Adding Flink parallelism past the topic's partition count does what?
opts: Doubles throughput for every extra task
check.why: Each partition is read by one source subtask; extra subtasks get nothing to read.

work: Open the simulator's partitions and hot key challenges.
Check skew across subtasks in your busiest job.

reels.title: Flink, Spark or a batch job?

beats.say: Your team asks for Flink. Is it the right call?
Pick Flink when sub-second answers change a decision, the event-time logic is complex, or state is huge. Pick Spark when the team lives on Spark and seconds are fine.

show.title: Choose by need
items: Flink: milliseconds, complex time, big state
Spark: seconds, one engine with batch

beats.say: If consumers read the numbers once an hour, a batch job every few minutes is cheaper, easier to test and easier to backfill. Say that out loud in interviews.
Managed services such as Confluent Cloud for Flink or Amazon's managed Flink remove operations, at a higher unit price. Choose them when nobody can own on-call.

check.q: Dashboards are read hourly. What is usually the best engine?
opts: A Flink job with a one second checkpoint
check.why: When minutes are fine, a scheduled batch is cheaper and simpler to test and backfill.

work: For each stream job, write the freshness its readers need.
Move one minutes-fresh job to a scheduled batch.

reels.title: Owning and paying for stream jobs

beats.say: Who pays for three hundred stream jobs that never stop?
A platform team runs the clusters, state storage and deployment path. Domain teams own their jobs, their state size and their service levels.
Streaming pays for compute every hour of the day, plus checkpoint storage. Show the bill per job so owners see it.
Move off when needs relax to minutes, when a managed service is cheaper than your on-call, or when a streaming table does the job.

check.q: Why does streaming often cost more than batch for the same data?
opts: Its compute runs all day, not only during a run
It always stores three times more data
It cannot use object storage at all
check.why: Stream jobs pay for always-on compute; batch jobs pay only while they run.

work: Add a cost per job to your streaming dashboard.
Name an owner and an SLO for every stream job.
